Thenceforth
THENS-forth
adv.
From thence and forth: from that time onward. Webster 1828: from that time. It marks a boundary after which a thing is permanently different, and our Lord uses it of salt that has lost its savour.

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

The word draws a line that does not move. Our Lord uses it of a disciple who has lost the thing that made him useful: Ye are the salt of the earth: but if the salt have lost his savour, wherewith shall it be salted? it is thenceforth good for nothing, but to be cast out, and to be trodden under foot of men (Matthew 5:13). The severity is in that one adverb. Salt without savour is not diminished salt; it is thenceforth good for nothing at all, and the only remaining use is the road. The Levitical law uses it for the point at which an animal becomes acceptable: from the eighth day and thenceforth it shall be accepted for an offering made by fire unto the LORD (Leviticus 22:27) — before that day, not acceptable; after it, acceptable. God’s appointments have thresholds. Chronicles marks the turn in Hezekiah’s standing after the deliverance from Sennacherib: so that he was magnified in the sight of all nations from thenceforth (2 Chronicles 32:23). And John records the exact point at which Pilate’s resistance began and, in the next breath, why it failed: And from thenceforth Pilate sought to release him: but the Jews cried out, saying, If thou let this man go, thou art not Caesar's friend (John 19:12).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines THENCEFORTH as from that time; from that time forward — marking the beginning of a new and continuing condition.

expand to see more

THENCEFORTH, adv. — From that time.

From that time forward; thereafter continually.

THENCEFORWARD, adv. — From that time onward; of the same force.

THENCE, adv. — From that place; from that time; for that reason.

From thence, Anglo-Saxon thanon, and forth.

Key Scripture

Matthew 5:13 — "Ye are the salt of the earth: but if the salt have lost his savour, wherewith shall it be salted? it is thenceforth good for nothing, but to be cast out, and to be trodden under foot of men."

Leviticus 22:27 — "When a bullock, or a sheep, or a goat, is brought forth, then it shall be seven days under the dam; and from the eighth day and thenceforth it shall be accepted for an offering made by fire unto the LORD."

2 Chronicles 32:23 — "And many brought gifts unto the LORD to Jerusalem, and presents to Hezekiah king of Judah: so that he was magnified in the sight of all nations from thenceforth."

John 19:12 — "And from thenceforth Pilate sought to release him: but the Jews cried out, saying, If thou let this man go, thou art not Caesar's friend: whosoever maketh himself a king speaketh against Caesar."

Modern Corruption

Matthew 5:13 says savourless salt is thenceforth good for nothing, which is not a threat of lost salvation but a warning that a church indistinguishable from the world has forfeited the only use it had.

expand to see more

Salt preserves and it stings; those are the two things it does, and both depend on its being unlike what it is put into. A church that sets out to become indistinguishable from the surrounding culture — in its ethics, its vocabulary, its estimate of what is shameful — has not become more useful to that culture but less, and Christ’s verdict is that it is thenceforth good for nothing but to be trodden under foot. The strategy of relevance has this exactly backwards: what the world needs from the church is precisely what the church is tempted to file off. Nor is this a warning aimed only at obviously liberal denominations; the same savourlessness arrives wherever a congregation’s distinctives are quietly retired to avoid friction. The passage is not teaching that a regenerate man can lose his salvation — the dictionary holds perseverance of the saints — but that a profession which no longer differs is a profession good for nothing.

Leviticus 22:27 is a small verse with a large principle: God appoints thresholds, and before the threshold the offering is simply not accepted. Seven days under the dam, and from the eighth day it may be brought. Nothing about the animal changes on the eighth morning except that God has said so, which is the whole point — acceptability is determined by God’s appointment and not by the worshipper’s estimate of sufficiency. This is the regulative principle in seed form, and it is the same logic that governs the ordinances of the New Testament church. John 19:12 shows what happens to a man who sees the right course and is governed by what a crowd may say of him: from thenceforth Pilate sought to release Him, and did not.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek eti and ek toutou, from this point; Hebrew halah (H1973), onward, thenceforth; maalah, upward and onward in time.

expand to see more

Greek ek toutou — from this, thenceforth; the turn in Pilate’s conduct (John 19:12).

Greek eti (G2089) — yet, still, any longer; the force of thenceforth good for nothing (Matthew 5:13).

Hebrew halah (H1973) — onward, further, thenceforth; from the eighth day and thenceforth (Leviticus 22:27).

Greek moraino (G3471) — to make foolish or insipid; the losing of savour in Matthew 5:13.

Hebrew ratsah (H7521) — to be pleased with, to accept favourably; the acceptance granted from the eighth day.

Usage

"It is thenceforth good for nothing, but to be cast out (Matthew 5:13) — savourless salt is not diminished salt; it is useless salt."

"From the eighth day and thenceforth it shall be accepted (Leviticus 22:27) — God appoints thresholds, and they are not negotiable."

"And from thenceforth Pilate sought to release him (John 19:12) — he saw the right course and was governed by the crowd."
